data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological natural selection has no 'goal' of truth, whereas Popperian science explicitly aims at verisimilitude.","In engineering, past performance is statistically correlated with future performance (induction works), whereas Popper denies this logical link in fundamental physics.","A survivor of a trial in biology is 'fit' for reproduction; a survivor of a test in Popper is merely 'not yet falsified', which is a weaker state."],"overturn_conditions":["If it can be shown that acting on a theory necessarily involves a bet on its future truth, the analogy to pure critical selection breaks.","If the 'goal' of action is proven to be distinct from the 'goal' of science (truth), the transfer of the selection rule is invalid."],"shared_structure":["Selection based on severity of past trials rather than frequency of success.","Distinction between 'fitness for purpose' (testing) and 'probability of recurrence'.","Rationality defined as adherence to a methodological rule rather than optimization of expected utility."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_003","SRC_007"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we choose the most stress-tested bridge design not because it is guaranteed to hold, but because it has revealed the most about structural limits, scientists choose corroborated theories to reveal the most about nature's limits.","The 'preference' is a procedural mandate for critical engagement, not an epistemic endorsement of truth."]},"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms without smuggling in induction, provided the preference is interpreted as a rational choice of the 'best tested' critical target rather than a probabilistic prediction of future success. The cost of this defense is the abandonment of any claim that science converges toward truth or that acting on a theory implies an expectation of its practical reliability; it merely implies an expectation of its high informational content and susceptibility to further refutation.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent's goal is explicitly short-term survival or practical utility defined independently of truth-content (e.g., building a bridge that won't collapse tomorrow), Popper's logic fails to provide a non-inductive bridge to preferring the tested theory over an untested one with equal logical probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on a theory' logically entails an implicit belief in its future reliability (as critics like Wesley Salmon argue), then Popper's distinction between corroboration and probability collapses into pragmatic induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'rationality' requires a positive reason to believe a theory will work (rather than just a negative reason that it hasn't failed yet), the Popperian preference is irrational.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Reframe 'preference for action' not as an inductive inference (Past Success -> Future Reliability) but as a deductive selection rule: Given the goal of maximizing error-elimination (verisimilitude), rational agents must select the theory with the highest empirical content (most severely tested and surviving) as the basis for action, because only such a theory offers the possibility of learning something new if it fails. Acting on a less corroborated theory is irrational not because it is likely false, but because it is less informative and thus less useful for the growth of knowledge, even in practical contexts where 'knowledge growth' is the proxy for 'problem solving'.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
